opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that it was a mix of infrastructure, data, and, frankly, conviction. Back around 2017, 2018, when we were doing some of the early imitation learning work, we saw signs that if you collected demonstrations carefully, a fairly simple behavior cloning policy could actually do surprisingly reasonable things on real robots. But the bottleneck was data collection. Every demonstration was expensive. You had to teleoperate the robot, the interfaces were clunky, and you'd get maybe a few dozen or a couple hundred trajectories for a task. So the results looked fragile, and it was hard to tell whether the method was limited or the data was.

The second part was the prevailing view in the community. At the time, a lot of people believed behavior cloning was fundamentally flawed because of compounding errors and distribution shift. The theory said it shouldn't scale well, so the natural reaction was to add more structure: hierarchical decompositions, task graphs, reinforcement learning on top, interactive corrections. I spent a good amount of my PhD on that structured direction, and I still think a lot of those ideas are valuable. But it meant that instead of doubling down on "let's just get way more data and bigger models," we kept trying to engineer around the problem.

And then there were the model architectures. We didn't yet have expressive policy classes like diffusion policies or large transformers that could capture multimodal human behavior well. If people demonstrate a task in several different ways, a naive regression policy averages them and does something weird. So some of the failures we attributed to behavior cloning itself were really failures of the function approximator.

Looking back, the evidence was there, but we didn't have scalable data pipelines, the right model classes, or the collective belief that scale would carry us. Once things like better teleoperation hardware, large shared datasets, and more expressive generative policies came together, the same basic idea suddenly looked very different. So I'd say the lesson for me was to take simple results more seriously and ask what it would take to scale them, rather than immediately assuming they need to be fixed with more complexity.

r001.rationale: The response cites infrastructure, data, community beliefs, and model architectures as limitations, but does not identify a lack of a hypothesis about which research direction to pursue.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose distributing exploration of different behavior-cloning research directions across a large research team.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest limitation was that the evidence was so narrow. We showed that behavior cloning worked on a handful of tasks, with a few hundred demonstrations, in fairly controlled settings. That's encouraging, but it doesn't tell you much about what happens when you try to scale, because the failure modes of imitation learning don't really show up until you push on the distribution. Compounding errors, the agent drifting into states it's never seen, the demonstrator being inconsistent across episodes. All of that was mostly hidden in those early experiments.

The second thing was data. In NLP or vision, you can go scrape the internet. In robotics, every demonstration is somebody standing there teleoperating a robot, and that's slow and expensive. So we had this result that said "more demos help," and no realistic path to getting ten or a hundred times more of them. It became very tempting to add structure to compensate, hierarchy, task representations, planners on top, and some of that was genuinely useful, but a lot of it was really us working around the fact that we couldn't just collect the data we needed.

And the third piece, which I think I underestimated at the time, was evaluation. We didn't have good ways to measure generalization. Success rate on the training task distribution looks great and tells you almost nothing about whether the policy understands anything. So even when we had positive results, it was hard to know what to build next, because we couldn't cleanly separate "this failed because of the algorithm" from "this failed because of the data" or "this failed because the task was ill-defined."

If I'm being self-critical, there was also a mindset issue. The community, me included, was a bit skeptical that something as simple as supervised learning on demonstrations could be the answer. So we kept looking for the clever algorithmic fix instead of asking what it would take to make the simple thing work at scale. In hindsight, the simple thing mostly needed more diverse data and better infrastructure, and that's not a very glamorous research agenda, which is maybe why it took a while.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest limitation was that we could get behavior cloning to work in a fairly narrow setting, but we didn’t really know how to build on that reliably. If the robot got into a situation that wasn’t represented in the demonstrations, it could make a small mistake, and that mistake would put it even further outside the data. So a successful demonstration didn’t necessarily tell us how close we were to a robust system.

And the obvious answer was to collect more data, but collecting robot demonstrations takes a lot of effort. You have to decide what variation to cover and how to capture the recovery behaviors, too. We had evidence that the approach could work, but we didn’t yet have a clear, practical way to turn that evidence into something much more general.

r001.rationale: The response describes difficulty generalizing behavior cloning and collecting more demonstrations, but does not identify lacking a hypothesis about which research direction to pursue.

r002.rationale: The response does not propose distributing exploration of research directions across a large team.

sol-6.1.text: I think the biggest limitation was that we didn’t really know how to scale it. We could get behavior cloning to work in a fairly constrained setting, but collecting demonstrations was expensive, and it was hard to tell how much more data we needed—or what kind of data would actually help. If the robot made a small mistake and ended up in a situation that wasn’t in the demonstrations, it often didn’t know how to recover. So we had evidence that the approach could work, but we didn’t yet have a clear recipe for turning that into something robust and general.

r001.rationale: It describes uncertainty about scaling, data needs, and robustness, but does not identify a lack of a hypothesis about which research direction to pursue.
